title: Fleeing yourself
hook: restless people keep changing places, fleeing themselves (On Tranquility 2)

segments.voice: Yesterday: Serenus asks for help, seasick on a calm sea. Your line was neither sick nor well. Did you say your honest sentence to someone, or to paper? Day four hundred ninety-six.
screen: `SERENUS ASKS FOR HELP — NEITHER SICK NOR WELL.`

segments.voice: Three in the morning, and you can't sleep. You lie on your left side. Too warm. You flip the pillow. Now the right side. Now your back. Each new position feels like the answer for about ninety seconds. Seneca uses exactly this picture. In the second chapter of On Tranquility, he stops listening to Serenus' symptoms and starts naming the illness. People who are restless, he says, behave like the sleepless: they keep turning over, trying one position after another, until they finally give up from exhaustion rather than rest. Today: fleeing yourself.
screen: `THREE A.M., TURNING OVER.` → `EACH POSITION, NINETY SECONDS.` → `SENECA NAMES THE ILLNESS.`

segments.voice: First, the root. Seneca says the trouble is a quiet dislike of yourself. Not hatred. More like boredom with your own company. A mind that can't settle with itself goes looking for somewhere else to be. Second, the trips. Seneca sketches the restless Roman: let's go to the seaside. No, too much luxury there, let's see the wild hills. No, too rough, back to the city, I've missed the noise. Every move is a new position in bed. Third, the poet's line. Seneca quotes the Roman poet Lucretius, in six words of Latin: hoc se quisque modo fugit. Thus each person flees himself. And then Seneca adds his own sharp question: but what good does it do, if you can't escape? You go along as your own companion, the very one you're running from. Back on day four hundred fifty-seven, a letter said you take yourself along. The essay goes one step further: the running is itself the symptom. Fourth, the cure begins with stopping. Seneca will offer remedies in the coming chapters: work, friends, simplicity, rest. But none of them work while you're still fleeing. The first move is the unglamorous one: stay put, and get to know the person you keep trying to leave behind. Many traditions keep a version of this. Desert monks were told to sit in their cell, and the cell would teach them everything. Seneca's version is a Roman one, but the bed and the 3 a.m. are the same everywhere.
screen: `A QUIET DISLIKE OF YOURSELF.` · `SEASIDE, HILLS, CITY, AGAIN.` · `HOC SE QUISQUE MODO FUGIT.` · `THE CURE BEGINS WITH STOPPING.` · then, large: `STAY PUT.`

segments.voice: For these two minutes, don't change position at all. Pick how you're sitting or lying, and stay. When an itch comes, notice it. When the urge to check something comes, notice it. When the thought 'this is boring' comes, notice that too, and stay. You're keeping company with the one person you can't leave. Be a polite host. Ask yourself, gently: what are you hoping to get away from? The bell holds the time.
Fleeing yourself. In Seneca's essay, the restless keep changing places, like a sleepless person turning over, and take themselves everywhere they go. Today's word.
Your line: stay put. Choose one hour today and stay in one place, doing one thing. No switching rooms, apps or plans. See who turns up. Day four hundred ninety-six.

howItsDone: People following Seneca's advice sometimes practice staying in one place, doing one thing, for a set time, to notice the urge to flee without obeying it.

fork.setup: you're a restless Roman. the seaside bored you, the hills were too rough, the city's too loud. what does Seneca say next?
options: stop running; you take yourself along.
fork.reveal: he quotes Lucretius and asks what good it does to flee, if you go along as your own companion.

original.note: Latin, Lucretius quoted by Seneca: 'thus each person flees himself'.

trapdoor: what you thought: restless people need a change of scene.
what it means: the restlessness comes along; Seneca says the cure starts with staying put.

what a scholar hears: Seneca's diagnosis, 'displicentia sui', dissatisfaction with oneself, and his quotation of Lucretius, On the Nature of Things 3.1068, borrow from an Epicurean poet for a Stoic point.
